newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Lithuania independence hero hails comeback victory.
newsitem.headline: Lithuania independence hero hails comeback victory.

text.p: Lithuanian independence leader Vytautas Landsbergis made a spectacular political comeback on Monday when his party emerged clear winner of a second round of parliamentary elections.
Landsbergis sealed his return to power four years after being rejected by voters in favour of his old foes, the ex-Communists of the Lithuanian Democratic Labour Party (LDLP).
"We are going to work, we do not have time to celebrate," Landsbergis, a stocky, stoop-shouldered ex-music professor, told journalists with a grin.
Landsbergis is expected to become Speaker of the new parliament, which some commentators say will allow him to prepare for a fight for the presidency in 1998.
He told a news conference that his Homeland Union party won 35 seats of the 65 in contention in the second round, adding to the 35 already won in the first round on October 20.
This falls short of an outright majority in the 141-seat parliament, but the Homeland Union has already pledged to form a coalition government with the Christian Democrats.
They won a total of 16 seats in the two rounds, meaning the coalition has a comfortable majority.
As in the first round, Sunday's poll was marked by voter apathy. Officials said that around 40 percent of people voted compared with 52 percent in the first round.
The results marked a remarkable comeback by Landsbergis, who came to be most closely associated with Lithuania's 1990-91 bid for independence.

He and thousands of ordinary Lithuanians refused to back down even after 13 people were killed in a Soviet army assault on Vilnius television tower in January 1991, one of the bloodiest incidents to accompany the collapse of Soviet power.
But the LDLP swept to victory in 1992 as the economy collapsed and Landsbergis' Sajudis independence movement tore itself apart with faction fighting.

The LDLP sealed its victory in 1993 when its leader, Algirdas Brazauskas, was elected president. It also started a trend in Eastern Europe, where ex-communists were often propelled back to power by people wearied by economic hardship.
The LDLP in 1996 won only 10 seats in the first round of the latest elections and just two in the second.

A Homeland Union government is expected to pursue the course of integration with the European Union (EU) and NATO followed by the LDLP but some aspects of economic policy, such as the push to unpeg the litas currency from the dollar, are worrying foreign investors.
But the party has tried to reassure that it is genuinely reform-minded.
"There cannot be any talk of slowing down the speed of reforms," Gediminas Vagnorius, the Homeland Union's candidate for prime minister, told the news conference.
Western diplomats have also said that Landsbergis, noted for his sharp tongue and sarcastic nature despite his mild-mannered appearance, will have to tone down his rhetoric.
Landsbergis has just as openly attacked the West for failing quickly to accept Lithuania into its security structures as he has his old enemy Russia for being imperialistic.
